title: From Temple to Rabbis
objective: After this level you can explain how rabbis, synagogues and the Talmud let Judaism thrive without a Temple, in a worldwide diaspora.
summary: After 70 CE, the Yavneh academy and the synagogue carried Judaism on through prayer, study and a minyan of ten. The oral law, gathered in the Mishnah, grew into the Talmud.

cards.headline: The Temple was gone. How do you keep a religion going without its center?
cards.body: In 70 CE the Romans destroyed the Second Temple, the only place for Jewish sacrifices. The answer that followed needed no building in Jerusalem at all: teachers, prayer and a library of arguments.

cards.headline: Out in a coffin
cards.body: Rabbi Johanan ben Zakkai's disciples are credited with smuggling their teacher out of Jerusalem in a coffin. He set up an academy at Jabneh (Yavneh), and ruled that ceremonies once limited to the Temple could be kept elsewhere, "to serve as memorials of the Sanctuary." With that, he fixed the conditions for Judaism to carry on after the Temple.

cards.headline: Ten people, anywhere
cards.body: The synagogue became the focal point of Jewish religious life. Its Hebrew names say what it's for: house of prayer, house of assembly, house of study. Its worship has no sacrifice, so it needs no priest. It needs a minyan, a quorum of ten, traditionally men (Reform and Conservative Judaism also count women); without one, there is no public Torah reading. That suited the Diaspora, Jewish communities scattered far beyond the land.

cards.headline: A library of arguments
cards.body: By 100 CE, rabbi, "my teacher", meant a sage who interprets Jewish law. Early in the 3rd century, Judah ha-Nasi gave final form to the Mishnah, the oldest authoritative collection of Jewish oral law. Later sages added the Gemara, a commentary, and together they make up the Talmud, where scholars debate every text to wring out its meaning.

mascot.line: Keep this pair straight: the Mishnah is the core text; the Talmud is the Mishnah plus the Gemara's debates about it.

cards.headline: From Temple to Rabbis: the takeaways
learned: Johanan ben Zakkai's academy at Yavneh carried Judaism past the Temple
The synagogue needs no priest, only a minyan of ten
The Mishnah plus the Gemara make up the Talmud

questions.prompt: After leaving Jerusalem, where did Johanan ben Zakkai set up his academy?

options.label: In Babylon, beside the exiles
options.rationale: His academy was in the land itself.

options.label: On Mount Sinai
options.rationale: That is where the Bible places the giving of the law.

questions.explanation: He set up an academy at Jabneh (Yavneh), fixing the conditions for Judaism after the Temple.
